newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GOVT TO DEBATE WAGES, IMPORTS APRIL 16 - AGENCY.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GOVT TO DEBATE WAGES, IMPORTS APRIL 16 - AGENCY.

text.p: The Czech government will meet on April 16 to discuss taking measures aimed at slowing down wage growth, state budget expenditure and imports, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus was quoted by CTK news agency as saying.
"The government has the aim to bring a certain package of measures on April 16," Klaus was quoted by CTK as telling Czech radio.
Klaus said wage growth had to be slowed down, but warned that the task would be tough due to low unemployment, it said,

He added that the way to tackle the problem would be through negotiations with employers and unions, slowing wage increases in sectors controlled by the state, and by less assistance to troubled industrial companies.
Klaus did not eleborate further what the measures should include.

But he once again took a shot at the Czech National Bank (CNB), saying its restrictive monetary policy was "terribly easy" to do, while "the art was to slow down, but not kill the economic growth at the same time".
The government has forecast wages will grow over 13 percent this year. Nominal gross wages grew 18 percent in 1996, and 15.2 percent, year on year, in the first two months of 1997.
CNB governor Josef Tosovsky last month said wage growth was a key problem for the economy and said it could not afford more than a nominal 10 percent rise in pay in 1997.
Meanwhile, the foreign trade deficit showed a 27.2 billion crown deficit in January and February, up from 16.2 billion deficit in the same period of 1996.
Finance Minster Ivan Kocarnik has said he would submit a plan this month to cut budget spending by two percent across the board in order keep the budget in balance.
State finances showed an 8.5 billion crown gap at the end of March, after a 1.7 bilion surplus in the same period of 1996.

The full-year budget was approved as balanced with revenues and expendiutures at 549.1 billion crowns. Last year's budget closed with a 1.56 billion deficit despite several rounds of spending cuts done during the year.
